title: Stranger Danger!
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the "stranger danger" moral panic that gripped America from the late 1970s into the 1980s. They cover FBI missing-persons statistics showing abduction by strangers is extremely rare, the 1979 disappearance of Etan Patz and the 1981 Adam Walsh abduction and murder, the milk carton campaign that began with Johnny Gosh and Eugene Martin in Iowa, and the debunked "Bonnie Lowman" internet legend. They discuss criticism from Dr. Benjamin Spock, the culture of fear and its effects on children and adults, the children's independent mobility research, racial disparities in missing-child media coverage, sex offender registry expansion after the Jacob Wetterling Act, UK campaigns like Clever Never Goes, the shift toward teaching body autonomy, and the Amber Alert system. The episode ends with a listener email from an Army veteran.

entities.name: National Center for Missing and Exploited Children

segments.title: Opening banter and framing
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with music chat, then introduce stranger danger as a misguided early-1980s campaign and discuss how Christian conservatives and the broader culture both fed the moral panics of the decade.

segments.title: Missing children statistics and abduction odds
segments.summary: They cite FBI National Crime Information Center figures for 2019 and calculate the very small odds of a child being abducted or murdered by a stranger, arguing the fear far outweighed the risk. Trends show kidnappings have declined and recovery rates have risen.

segments.title: Media coverage and family abuse
segments.summary: They note newspapers focused on strangers while family members and acquaintances are the far more common threat in child sexual abuse. The hosts briefly discuss the documentary Abducted in Plain Sight.

segments.title: Etan Patz disappearance
segments.summary: Etan Patz, a six-year-old, vanished in May 1979 walking alone to a bus stop in Soho. The case became a national news story. Pedro Hernandez confessed in 2012 and was convicted in 2017, but the case is considered unresolved, and a civil suit was won against Jose Ramos.

segments.title: Adam Walsh abduction
segments.summary: Adam Walsh was abducted in 1981 from a Sears store in Hollywood, Florida, while his mother shopped nearby. His head was found in a canal about ten days later, which cemented national fear of stranger abduction.

segments.title: Milk carton campaign origins
segments.summary: The milk carton campaign began in Iowa with Johnny Gosh and Eugene Martin, both paperboys in Des Moines. Anderson Erickson Dairy is credited with first printing missing children on milk cartons in 1984. The effort spread to Chicago, California, and nationally through the National Child Safety Council, fading by the mid-1990s.

segments.title: Bonnie Lowman internet legend
segments.summary: The hosts examine a popular story about Bonnie Lowman who recognized her own face on a milk carton. Searches of major newspapers found nothing, and the story appears repeated on low-credibility sites, so they conclude it is likely an internet legend.

segments.title: Culture of fear and fingerprinting
segments.summary: Dr. Benjamin Spock criticized the climate of fear in a Washington Post piece. Josh and Chuck recall Saturday morning PSAs, child fingerprinting fairs, and the Washington Post's examples of children terrorized by fear. A survey found that many adults would not help a child in need.

segments.title: Children's independent mobility and community effects
segments.summary: They discuss children's independent mobility, which correlates with psychological, analytical, and motor development. Fear has made adults wary of interacting with children, eroding community child-rearing, and it has also affected the Boy Scouts' lost-child practices.

segments.title: Sex offender registries and the Jacob Wetterling Act
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Jacob Wetterling Act and the Sex Offender Registry, Jacob's mother's later regret about overly broad registries, and examples of minor offenses that can lead to registration. They note the problem of residency restrictions that push offenders into homelessness.

segments.title: Clever Never Goes, body autonomy, and Amber Alert
segments.summary: They cover the UK's Clever Never Goes campaign, the UK's Charlie Says PSAs, the shift toward teaching children body autonomy and sexual abuse awareness, and the Amber Alert system named after Amber Hagerman, which they credit with recovering about a thousand children.

segments.title: Listener mail from an Army veteran
segments.summary: A listener who is a former Army paratrooper and medic writes about how the show has helped during a divorce and career loss. The hosts respond warmly.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode, mention how to contact the show, and sign off with the 'Stuff You Should Know' tagline.
